title: API 510 Training in Houston: Pressure Vessel Exam Prep
description: Self-paced online API 510 exam prep for Houston candidates: Ship Channel columns, coke drums and exchangers, local damage mechanisms and instructor Q&A.
h1: API 510 Training in Houston: Online Exam Prep for Pressure Vessel Inspectors on the Ship Channel
html:
API 510 exam prep for Houston pressure vessel inspectors

Every refinery and chemical plant around the Houston Ship Channel is built from pressure vessels: crude towers, coke drums, reactors, separators, accumulators and the shells of heat exchangers. An API 510 inspector is the person the owner relies on to say whether each of them can keep running at its rating, needs a repair or must be rerated. This page is for candidates in Harris, Galveston, Chambers and Brazoria counties who are preparing for the API 510 Pressure Vessel Inspector examination, whether they work as NDT technicians, welders, operators, engineers or contract inspectors.

The Atlantis course is self-paced and online, with an instructor who answers your questions as you work through the codes. There is no Atlantis classroom in Houston. Atlantis has an office in Houston, yet a candidate in Baytown studies exactly the same material as one in Sugar Land or League City, on a schedule that suits their shift pattern. The American Petroleum Institute (API) sets the eligibility rules, administers the API 510 examination at Prometric test centres and issues the certification. The course prepares you for that examination; it does not count towards the experience API asks you to document.

Where API 510 inspectors work around Houston

The Energy Information Administration's survey of operable refineries as of January 2026 gives a dependable map of where crude is still processed near the city. The table lists the plants within reach of Houston with the operating company as EIA records it, the parent company in brackets where the two differ, and the processing units that generate the most vessel inspection.

Two ownership changes are worth knowing when you read job postings: Chevron bought the Pasadena refinery from Petrobras in 2019, and Shell completed the sale of its Deer Park refinery interest to its partner Pemex in 2022 while keeping full ownership of the Deer Park Chemicals plant next door.

Chemical plants add a second large population of vessels. ExxonMobil's 2026 fact sheet describes its Baytown complex as roughly 3,400 acres holding a refinery, a chemical plant and the Baytown Olefins Plant, with about 1,900 employees and an average of 4,800 contract personnel on site. Chevron Phillips Chemical's Cedar Bayou plant, also in Baytown, makes ethylene, normal alpha olefins, propylene and three grades of polyethylene. Olefins crackers, polymer reactors, quench towers and refrigeration drums are all API 510 equipment once they are in service.

The vessels a Houston API 510 inspector signs for

  • Columns and towers. Crude and vacuum towers, fractionators, strippers and absorbers, where shell thinning near liquid levels and feed nozzles is typical.
  • Coke drums. EIA lists delayed coking at Baytown, Deer Park, Galveston Bay, Texas City and Sweeny. Drums that are filled hot and quenched on every cycle tend to bulge and crack, so shell distortion surveys and weld inspection at the skirt are routine work for the inspectors assigned to those units.
  • Hydroprocessing reactors and separators. Hydrocracking capacity at Baytown, Deer Park and Galveston Bay means thick-walled vessels in hot hydrogen service, where high-temperature hydrogen attack and high-temperature H2/H2S corrosion are the mechanisms to screen.
  • Heat exchanger shells, channels and heads. NDT crews test the tubes; the API 510 inspector judges the pressure-retaining shell side and what the tube results mean for the next run.
  • Drums and accumulators in sour and amine service. Overhead accumulators, amine contactors and regenerators, sour water strippers and flare knock-out drums are where wet H2S damage and amine stress corrosion cracking turn up.
  • Boiler-side vessels. Deaerators, condensate drums and blowdown vessels sit beside the steam system; boiler water and steam condensate corrosion appears in the examination's damage-mechanism list for exactly this reason.
  • Pressure-relieving devices. API RP 576 is on the examination, so learn how relief valves are inspected, tested and recorded.

Houston damage mechanisms in the API 510 Body of Knowledge

The current API 510 Body of Knowledge limits API RP 571 questions to its definitions section and fifteen mechanisms. A Houston candidate has usually met most of them on the job, which helps, but the exam asks for RP 571's description: the affected materials, the critical factors, the appearance of the damage and the inspection methods. The table links each mechanism on the list to the local units where you are most likely to have seen it.

Atmospheric corrosion, boiler water and steam condensate corrosion and erosion/erosion-corrosion complete the list. Where your site's name for a problem differs from RP 571's, learn RP 571's terms, because those are the words the question uses.

Section VIII and API 510 calculations, with a Ship Channel example

Calculation questions concern existing vessels under internal pressure only, in US customary or SI units. The Body of Knowledge names the ones to practise: required thickness and part MAWP for cylindrical shells (UG-27) and for ellipsoidal and hemispherical heads (UG-32), joint efficiency from Table UW-12 and the radiography marks on a nameplate (UW-11), test pressure corrected for temperature (UG-99 and UG-100), impact-test exemption with UCS-66, and attachment weld sizes at openings (UW-16). Corrosion rates, remaining corrosion allowance, remaining life and inspection intervals come from API 510 itself, and API warns that their formulas may be asked closed-book.

Take a hypothetical overhead accumulator at a Ship Channel refinery: inside diameter 72 in., design pressure 250 psig, allowable stress given as 20,000 psi, and a nameplate showing spot radiography, so Table UW-12 gives E = 0.85 for its Type 1 longitudinal seams.

  1. Required shell thickness: t = PR / (SE − 0.6P) = 250 × 36 / (20,000 × 0.85 − 0.6 × 250) = 9,000 / 16,850 = 0.534 in.
  2. Corrosion rate: the shell read 0.750 in. eight years ago and 0.690 in. now, so (0.750 − 0.690) / 8 = 0.0075 in. per year.
  3. Remaining life: (0.690 − 0.534) / 0.0075 = 20.8 years.
  4. Internal inspection interval: API 510 allows the lesser of half the remaining life or ten years, so ten years governs here.

The common errors are using the diameter instead of the radius, taking E as 1.0 because the seams look sound, and forgetting that a drop in E after a rerate or repair changes every number that follows. Worked examples of this kind are a large part of the course, and the instructor answers questions on any step that will not come out. For more on the code itself, see the API 510 code explainer.

Owner-user inspection departments and contract inspectors

Much of Houston's vessel inspection is planned and approved by the owner-user's own inspection group, the department at each refinery or chemical plant that keeps the equipment files, sets intervals and signs repair and rerate documents. API 510 recognises an owner-user's inspection organisation as one kind of authorized inspection agency, alongside independent organisations working under contract to the owner, which is why both employers appear on the applications Houston candidates submit.

Contractors supply most of the extra people during turnarounds; firms headquartered in the area, Team, Inc. in Sugar Land among them, provide inspection, condition assessment, maintenance and repair services. If your experience is spread across several contractors and sites, keep a running log of the vessels you inspected and your role on each, signed by the supervisor at the time. API verifies experience, and a record rebuilt years later from memory is harder to support.

Routes into API 510 for Houston candidates

API matches education to experience: one year of inspection activity with an engineering or technology degree, two years with a two-year degree or certificate, three years with a high school diploma, and five or more with no formal education, gained in the last ten years while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency. The full scale and the wording API uses are on the API 510 certification requirements page.

  • NDT technicians on contractor crews often have years of thickness surveys and weld inspection on vessels already. ASNT training for those roles is described on the NDT training in Houston page.
  • Graduates of San Jacinto College's Fixed Equipment Inspection Technology degree will have taken pressure vessel inspection and pressure piping and valve inspection courses in their second year. Ask API whether your award counts towards the education tier before you rely on it.
  • Welders and welding inspectors can count repair and fabrication work on vessels; some take the welding inspector credential first, described on the CWI exam preparation page for Houston.
  • Operators and process technicians know their units well but need documented time supervising or performing inspection.
  • Engineers at owner-users reach eligibility after one year of inspection work with a bachelor's degree.

Studying for API 510 from a Houston job

The advantage of preparing while you work in a plant is that the paperwork the exam describes is all around you. Ask to read a manufacturer's data report and a vessel nameplate in your unit, find the radiography mark and the MDMT, and check whether you could defend the joint efficiency used in the last thickness calculation. Those habits turn the closed-book questions into recall rather than guesswork.

Because the course is self-paced, a candidate on a rotating schedule at a Pasadena or Texas City site can work through Section VIII on days off and slow down during a turnaround. If a practice answer seems to contradict what your unit actually does, send it to the instructor; the reply works from the code text, which is what the examination marks.

Other ways to prepare in Houston, compared honestly

  • College programmes. San Jacinto College and Lone Star College run inspection technology programmes over several terms; they suit people early in their careers rather than one exam window.
  • In-person exam-prep classes. Private training companies run them on fixed dates, which suits candidates who can take the time off but is hard to fit around a turnaround.
  • Employer mentoring. Valuable experience beside a certified inspector, though it rarely covers every code section the exam samples.
  • The Atlantis course. Self-paced study with instructor Q&A, practice papers in the exam's two-part format and no fixed dates. Fees are quoted on request.

Sitting the exam and sponsoring candidates

Once API accepts your application you book a seat in Prometric's system; Prometric lists test centres in and around Houston. The day runs about 7.5 hours, closed-book first and open-book after lunch, with the code PDFs on the computer and nothing of your own allowed in the room. Try not to book it the morning after a night shift.

Owner-users and contractors in the Houston area can enrol several API 510 candidates at once, including candidates for different API exams. The most useful thing an employer can do is sign accurate experience records promptly and keep the candidate off the turnaround roster during the exam window. See the API exam schedule for windows and deadlines.

faq.q: Can I attend an API 510 class in Houston in person?
faq.a: Not with Atlantis. There is no Atlantis classroom in Houston, although Atlantis has an office there. The API 510 course is self-paced and online, and an instructor answers your questions as you study, which suits shift work and turnaround travel along the Ship Channel. The examination itself is the only in-person part: you sit it at a Prometric test centre after API approves your application.

faq.q: Do coke drum and hydrocracker topics come up on the API 510 exam?
faq.a: Not by unit name. The examination tests API 510, the listed sections of API RP 571 and the other documents in the Body of Knowledge. Several listed mechanisms, such as high-temperature hydrogen attack, high-temperature H2/H2S corrosion and sulfidation, are exactly what Houston inspectors meet in hydroprocessing and coking units, so field experience helps, but the answer must come from RP 571's wording rather than site practice.

faq.q: Does contract inspection on Ship Channel turnarounds count toward API 510 eligibility?
faq.a: It can, if the work was supervising or performing inspection activities on pressure vessels as API 510 describes them and you were employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency at the time. API verifies the experience you document, so keep dates, sites, equipment and your role for each assignment, and ask a supervisor who saw the work to confirm it. The certification requirements page summarises the rules.

faq.q: Which Section VIII calculations should a Houston candidate practise most?
faq.a: UG-27 shell thickness and part MAWP, UG-32 head thickness for ellipsoidal and hemispherical heads, Table UW-12 joint efficiency with the nameplate radiography marks, UG-99 and UG-100 test pressure corrected for temperature, UCS-66 impact-test exemption and UW-16 weld sizes at openings. Add the API 510 corrosion rate, remaining life and interval rules, which may be asked closed-book. Practise each in both US customary and SI units.

faq.q: I already hold API 570. Is API 510 worth adding in Houston?
faq.a: For many unit inspectors it is, because a process unit is vessels joined by piping and contractors can then assign one person to both scopes. The two examinations share API RP 571, RP 577 and RP 578, ASME Section V and IX and PCC-2, though the RP 571 mechanism lists differ, so part of your study carries over. The new material is mainly API 510 itself, ASME Section VIII Division 1 and RP 572.

faq.q: Does a San Jacinto College inspection degree replace API 510 exam prep?
faq.a: No; the two do different jobs. A college programme teaches inspection over several terms and can help you qualify for the education part of API's scale, if API accepts the award as engineering or technology. Exam prep focuses on the specific documents, editions and question styles of your exam window. Many candidates finish a degree, gain experience on the job and then prepare for the exam itself.

faq.q: Can a Baytown or Pasadena employer enrol several API 510 candidates?
faq.a: Yes. An owner-user or contractor can sponsor a group, and the group can mix API 510 with other API exams. Fees are quoted on request. Each candidate studies at their own pace, asks the instructor their own questions and applies to API individually. Tell us the number of candidates and the windows they are aiming for when you enquire.

faq.q: Where do Houston candidates sit the API 510 exam?
faq.a: At a Prometric test centre, booked after API approves the application; Prometric lists centres in and around Houston. The computer-based exam has 170 questions, 110 closed-book and 60 open-book, over a day of about 7.5 hours including a short tutorial and a lunch break. For the open-book part the code documents are on screen, and you may not bring books or notes.
